title: Pulmonary Function Tests: Obstruction, Restriction, Diffusion, and Clinical Fit
bottomLine: Interpret spirometry in sequence: confirm technical quality, decide whether obstruction is present using an appropriate lower-limit-of-normal framework, assess bronchodilator response when relevant, and use lung volumes/DLCO when restriction or gas-transfer disease is suspected. A PFT pattern supports physiology; it does not name the disease by itself.
recognize: Obstruction is identified from expiratory flow relationships rather than low FEV1 alone.
A low FVC can reflect restriction, air trapping or suboptimal effort; true restriction requires reduced total lung capacity.
DLCO can help separate parenchymal, pulmonary vascular and emphysematous physiology when interpreted with hemoglobin and lung-volume context.
differentiate: Bronchodilator reversibility supports variable airflow limitation but its absence does not exclude asthma.
Race-based correction should not be treated as biologic destiny; current CTS guidance emphasizes careful interpretation of reference equations and patient context.
Normal spirometry does not exclude episodic asthma, early interstitial disease or pulmonary vascular disease when the history is compelling.
assessment: Review smoking/vaping, occupational exposure, symptom variability, exertional limitation, inhaler use, recent infection and whether the patient could perform acceptable manoeuvres.
workup: Use spirometry first for common airflow questions; add lung volumes, DLCO, bronchoprovocation or exercise testing only when they answer a remaining clinical question.
management: Treat the diagnosed disease, not the spirometry label; unexpected or discordant patterns require repeat high-quality testing or respirology review.
medicationSafety: Do not escalate inhaled therapy solely from one poor-quality spirometry session.
Hold/continue bronchodilators before testing according to the laboratory protocol and clinical question rather than a universal rule.
redFlags: PFT result discordant with major clinical deterioration
counselling: Explain that PFTs measure how the lungs move and exchange gas; the pattern must still be matched to symptoms and other tests.
followUp: Repeat testing at intervals tied to diagnosis, treatment change or clinical decline—not simply because a prior value was abnormal.
examTrap: Calling a low FVC 'restriction' without measuring total lung capacity or considering air trapping/effort.
oneLinePearl: PFTs describe physiology first; disease labels come after the pattern is matched to the patient.
sourceBasis: Canadian Thoracic Society pulmonary-function-testing guidance and 2023 interpretation statement

title: Oxygen Therapy: Treat Hypoxemia, Prescribe a Target, Reassess the Cause
bottomLine: Oxygen is a drug for hypoxemia, not a routine treatment for breathlessness with normal oxygenation. Define the indication, delivery device and target saturation, recognize patients at risk of hypercapnic respiratory failure, and reassess whether oxygen is still needed after the acute illness changes.
recognize: Hypoxemia, not dyspnea severity alone, drives most oxygen decisions.
Some COPD/neuromuscular/chest-wall patients can retain carbon dioxide; worsening somnolence or acidosis after oxygen escalation requires ventilation assessment rather than simply removing all oxygen.
Long-term home oxygen eligibility requires stable chronic assessment rather than an isolated transient inpatient saturation.
differentiate: Oxygenation failure and ventilation failure are different problems; normal SpO2 does not exclude dangerous hypercapnia.
Palliative oxygen is not automatically superior to airflow/fan and symptom-directed therapy in a nonhypoxemic patient.
assessment: Assess SpO2, respiratory effort, mental status, perfusion and the underlying cause; obtain blood gas when hypercapnia or severe gas-exchange failure is plausible.
workup: Confirm persistent chronic hypoxemia under stable conditions before long-term oxygen prescription; use exertional/nocturnal testing when that specific indication is being evaluated.
management: Titrate oxygen to a documented target appropriate to the clinical syndrome and adjust the device to reliably achieve it.
Treat the cause in parallel and escalate to ventilatory support when oxygen alone cannot correct respiratory failure.
medicationSafety: Avoid unnecessary hyperoxia, especially in patients at risk for hypercapnic respiratory failure.
Home oxygen requires fire/smoking safety and equipment education.
redFlags: Unsafe smoking/open-flame exposure with home oxygen
counselling: Teach that oxygen treats low blood oxygen and does not replace inhalers, airway clearance or treatment of the underlying disease.
Review fire safety and device use before discharge.
followUp: Reassess oxygen need after recovery from acute illness and close the loop on home-oxygen qualification/testing where required.
examTrap: Giving oxygen automatically for dyspnea despite normal saturation—or stopping needed oxygen in a hypercapnic patient instead of correcting the ventilation problem safely.
oneLinePearl: Prescribe oxygen with an indication and a target; reassess because the need can change.
sourceBasis: Canadian Thoracic Society COPD/home respiratory support resources

title: Pulmonary Nodule: Risk-Stratify the Nodule, Do Not Turn Screening Into Diagnosis
bottomLine: A pulmonary nodule needs structured malignancy-risk assessment using size, morphology, growth, smoking/exposure history and patient factors. Screening pathways apply to asymptomatic eligible people; a symptomatic patient or a nodule already under surveillance belongs to a diagnostic pathway.
recognize: Growth, spiculation, upper-lobe location, larger size and higher clinical cancer risk increase concern.
Small stable nodules in low-risk patients may require little or no follow-up depending on the validated pathway.
Hemoptysis, unexplained weight loss or other cancer symptoms convert the problem from screening/surveillance to diagnostic evaluation.
differentiate: Granuloma/scar, infection and benign neoplasm can mimic malignancy.
A nodule found during lung-cancer screening is managed through the program's structured reporting pathway, while an incidental nodule may use validated incidental-nodule guidance.
assessment: Review age, smoking history, occupational/environmental exposure, prior cancer, immune status, previous imaging, symptoms and family history.
workup: Compare prior imaging before ordering new tests; use thin-section CT characterization and risk-based follow-up.
PET/biopsy/surgical referral is reserved for nodules whose size/risk/growth makes those tests clinically useful.
management: Document the surveillance interval and ownership of the next scan or referral.
Refer suspicious or growing nodules through lung diagnostic/respirology/thoracic pathways rather than repeatedly ordering CT without a definitive plan.
medicationSafety: Avoid unnecessary empiric antibiotics for an indeterminate nodule without a compatible infectious syndrome.
Consider anticoagulant/antiplatelet and comorbidity risk before invasive biopsy planning.
redFlags: New nodule in a patient with prior malignancy or major immunocompromise
counselling: Explain the estimated risk and why surveillance can be safer than immediate biopsy for some nodules.
Clarify who will track the next imaging date so follow-up is not lost.
followUp: Use closed-loop nodule tracking until surveillance ends or a definitive diagnosis is reached.
examTrap: Applying a routine lung-screening interval to a patient with hemoptysis and a suspicious nodule instead of switching to diagnostic evaluation.
oneLinePearl: Pulmonary nodules are risk-and-growth problems; symptoms override screening logic.
sourceBasis: Ontario Health (Cancer Care Ontario) lung diagnostic and screening pathways
Fleischner pulmonary-nodule measurement/follow-up principles where applicable

title: Respiratory Infection in Immunocompromise: Broaden the Differential, Escalate Earlier
bottomLine: In an immunocompromised patient, respiratory infection can progress rapidly, inflammatory signs can be muted, and the pathogen differential is wider. Stabilize first, define the immune defect/exposures, obtain appropriate microbiology and imaging early, and involve acute-care/infectious-disease/respirology teams when severity or opportunistic infection is plausible.
recognize: Fever may be absent despite serious infection; hypoxemia, tachypnea, new infiltrates or functional decline can be the first clue.
Neutropenia, transplant, prolonged corticosteroid/biologic therapy and advanced immune deficiency create different pathogen risks.
differentiate: Drug toxicity, pulmonary edema, malignancy and inflammatory lung disease can mimic infection.
A normal early chest x-ray does not exclude serious opportunistic pneumonia when symptoms and host risk are high.
assessment: Define immune defect, neutrophil status, transplant timing, medications, prophylaxis, prior organisms, travel/exposures, oxygenation and hemodynamic stability.
workup: Use early chest imaging and syndrome-directed blood/respiratory cultures, viral testing and opportunistic-pathogen testing; bronchoscopy/BAL may be required when noninvasive testing is insufficient.
management: Start prompt empiric therapy when severe infection or neutropenic sepsis is plausible, matched to the host, syndrome and local microbiology; narrow when diagnostic evidence permits.
Escalate hypoxemia, hemodynamic instability or rapidly progressive infiltrates to hospital-level care.
medicationSafety: Renal/hepatic function and major interactions are especially important because transplant/immunosuppressive regimens can interact with azoles, macrolides and other anti-infectives.
Do not stop essential immunosuppression abruptly without specialist guidance unless an emergency protocol directs it.
redFlags: Neutropenia with fever or respiratory symptoms
Possible Pneumocystis, invasive fungal or disseminated infection
counselling: Teach early reporting of fever, dyspnea and exposure risks because delay is more dangerous in immunocompromised hosts.
followUp: Close the loop on pending cultures/advanced testing and coordinate prophylaxis/immunosuppression adjustments with the specialty team.
examTrap: Reassuring an immunocompromised patient because they are afebrile and the first chest x-ray is normal despite progressive dyspnea and hypoxemia.
oneLinePearl: Immunocompromise lowers the threshold for imaging, microbiology and escalation because classic signs may be missing.
sourceBasis: Canadian Thoracic Society 2026 infection-screening position statement for immunosuppressed lung disease
Canadian infectious-disease and transplant practice principles

title: Thoracentesis: Diagnose or Drain the Pleural Space Safely
bottomLine: Thoracentesis is performed to diagnose an unexplained pleural effusion or relieve significant symptoms from a sizable effusion. Confirm the indication, use ultrasound guidance when available/standard, assess bleeding and respiratory risk, send fluid studies that answer the differential, and recognize pneumothorax, bleeding and re-expansion complications promptly.
recognize: New unilateral or unexplained exudative-appearing effusions commonly require diagnostic sampling.
Large symptomatic effusions can cause dyspnea and hypoxemia; urgent drainage depends on physiology and suspected cause.
Suspected complicated parapneumonic effusion/empyema changes management from simple diagnostic tap to drainage/source-control planning.
differentiate: Known stable bilateral heart-failure effusions may improve with treatment without immediate tap when the presentation is typical.
Transudate/exudate classification informs mechanism but does not replace cytology, microbiology or clinical context.
assessment: Assess respiratory status, effusion size/location, ultrasound window, anticoagulants/antiplatelets, bleeding disorder, skin infection and ability to cooperate/position safely.
workup: Use pleural protein/LDH with paired serum values when Light-type classification is relevant; add cell count, pH/glucose, culture or cytology according to the differential.
Post-procedure imaging is symptom/complication dependent rather than automatically required after every uncomplicated ultrasound-guided procedure.
management: Use a trained proceduralist and ultrasound-guided technique according to local policy.
Stop and reassess if the patient develops chest pain, persistent cough, dyspnea, hypotension or other signs of complication during drainage.
Empyema/complicated infection requires antibiotic plus drainage/source-control pathway.
medicationSafety: Anticoagulation/antiplatelet management is agent- and bleeding-risk specific; do not apply one universal hold interval.
Avoid overly rapid/large-volume removal without monitoring because re-expansion pulmonary edema is uncommon but serious.
redFlags: Post-procedure hypoxemia or pleuritic pain suggesting pneumothorax
Respiratory distress from a large effusion
counselling: Explain whether the procedure is diagnostic, therapeutic or both and what symptoms after the procedure require urgent reassessment.
followUp: Track fluid results to diagnostic resolution and ensure recurrent effusion has a cause-specific plan rather than repeated taps alone.
examTrap: Performing repeated therapeutic taps without investigating a recurrent unilateral effusion—or ordering routine post-tap chest x-ray after every uncomplicated ultrasound-guided procedure regardless of symptoms/local policy.
oneLinePearl: Thoracentesis should answer a question or relieve a physiologic burden—and its results need ownership.

title: Occupational Lung Disease: Diagnose the Exposure Pattern Before the Job Is Lost
bottomLine: Occupational lung disease is diagnosed by linking a credible workplace exposure to a compatible respiratory pattern and objective testing. Ask about the job early, document exposure and symptom timing carefully, and avoid advising permanent job removal before enough evidence is collected when continued exposure is not immediately dangerous.
recognize: Work-related asthma often improves away from work and worsens during shifts or work periods, but delayed reactions can blur the pattern.
Silica, asbestos, metal/wood dusts, fumes and sensitizers can cause interstitial, pleural, obstructive or malignant disease.
Coworker symptoms or a cluster can support an occupational exposure problem.
differentiate: Asthma worsened by irritants at work differs from true occupational asthma caused by a workplace sensitizer, though both matter clinically.
Smoking-related COPD can coexist with occupational exposure; one risk does not erase the other.
assessment: Take a chronological job/exposure history including tasks, materials, ventilation/PPE, spills, symptom timing, coworkers, hobbies and prior jobs.
Ask whether symptoms improve on weekends/vacations and document objective baseline before exposure changes when safe.
workup: Use spirometry and serial peak-flow or other objective testing across work/off-work periods when appropriate; refer for specialized bronchoprovocation or occupational-respirology assessment when diagnosis remains uncertain.
Use imaging, DLCO or disease-specific testing for suspected pneumoconiosis/ILD/pleural disease.
management: Reduce or eliminate harmful exposure when clinically indicated while coordinating occupational medicine, workplace controls and compensation processes.
Treat the respiratory disease according to standard guidance but recognize that medication cannot substitute for control of the causative exposure.
medicationSafety: Repeated systemic steroid treatment for work-triggered asthma without exposure control can mask ongoing injury and add toxicity.
Respiratory protection must be appropriate to the hazard; a generic mask is not a universal exposure solution.
redFlags: Continued exposure to a known high-risk sensitizer with severe asthma
counselling: Explain why detailed exposure documentation matters for both diagnosis and workplace protection.
Discuss work modification using non-stigmatizing, evidence-based recommendations and applicable occupational-health systems.
followUp: Reassess symptoms/lung function after exposure modification and close the loop on occupational-medicine/respirology referral.
examTrap: Telling a patient to quit their job immediately before collecting an adequate exposure history and objective work-related physiology when there is no acute danger.
oneLinePearl: For occupational lung disease, the exposure timeline is part of the diagnostic test.
sourceBasis: Canadian Thoracic Society occupational/asthma practice resources
